2027-05-06.title: Thursday of the Sixth Week of Easter
readings: Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla and worked with them, and every sabbath he argued in the synagogue
The Lord has revealed to the nations his saving power (or: Alleluia)
You will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy
2027-05-06.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. In India the Solemnity of the Ascension of the Lord is transferred to Sunday 9 May, so today the Easter weekday is celebrated with these readings. Where the Ascension is kept on this Thursday, the fortieth day after Easter (for example in the Vatican and a number of other countries), today is the Solemnity of the Ascension, a holy day of obligation there.
2027-05-06.verse: Very truly, I tell you, you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
theo: Paul has left Athens, where only a handful of people believed, and has come to Corinth. It was a very different city: a busy Roman colony on the narrow neck of land between two seas, with a harbour on each side, full of sailors, traders, slaves, soldiers and pilgrims to its temples. There Paul finds a Jewish couple, Aquila and Priscilla, “who had recently come from Italy … because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome.” The Roman historian Suetonius also mentions that expulsion, around the year 49. Paul goes to see them, “and, because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them.” They were tentmakers, workers in leather and cloth. The great apostle of the nations earns his bread with a needle and a knife in a workshop, and on the sabbath he goes to the synagogue “and would try to convince Jews and Greeks.” When Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia, perhaps bringing a gift from the Philippians, Paul is able to give himself entirely to “proclaiming the word, testifying to the Jews that the Messiah was Jesus.”

Not everyone welcomes the message. Some in the synagogue oppose Paul, and he makes a solemn gesture: he shakes out his clothes and declares that he is now going to the Gentiles. But notice where he goes: next door, to the house of Titius Justus, “a worshiper of God,” whose house stands right beside the synagogue. Paul does not walk away from his people in anger; he stays close. And the very next line tells us that “Crispus, the official of the synagogue, became a believer in the Lord, together with all his household,” and that “many of the Corinthians who heard Paul became believers and were baptized.” Years later Paul will remember that he baptized Crispus with his own hands (1 Corinthians 1:14). The reading is not a story of Jews against Christians: it is a story of one Jewish community in which some believed and some did not, and of a Jewish apostle, working beside Jewish friends, who opened the door of the Messiah to everyone. The Psalm sings the meaning of it: “All the ends of the earth have seen the victory of our God.”

The Gospel takes us back to the Last Supper. Jesus says something the disciples cannot understand: “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.” They whisper among themselves: “What does he mean by this ‘a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.” Jesus does not explain the timetable. He tells them what the waiting will feel like: “you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.” He does not say that the pain will be replaced by joy, as if it were thrown away; he says it will turn into joy, as the cross itself became the sign of victory. The first “little while” was the three days of the Passion. But the Fathers heard a second meaning too: the whole time of the Church, between the Ascension and the Lord's return, is also “a little while.” Today, in Rome and in many places, the Church celebrates the Ascension, the day the disciples stopped seeing Jesus with their eyes. In India we shall celebrate it on Sunday. Either way, we are the people of the little while: we do not yet see him, and we are learning, in work and witness like Paul's, to let our pains be turned into joy.
conn: A Roman colony and the capital of the province of Achaia, on the isthmus between the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf, with the ports of Lechaeum and Cenchreae. Paul stayed there about eighteen months (Acts 18:11) and later wrote at least two letters to its church.

A Jewish married couple, Aquila from Pontus on the Black Sea. Paul calls them “Prisca and Aquila, who work with me in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3). They are named six times in the New Testament, and Priscilla is usually named first.

The emperor Claudius (41–54) expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances, which Suetonius links to someone called “Chrestus,” probably a garbled form of Christus. The date is usually given as about AD 49.
The Greek skēnopoioi means makers of tents, probably working in leather. Paul supported himself by his trade so as not to be a burden to his churches (1 Thessalonians 2:9; Acts 20:34).

A prophetic gesture: I am not responsible for your refusal. Jesus told the Twelve to shake the dust from their feet where they were not received (Luke 9:5); Paul did so at Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51).
A God-fearing Gentile and the official of the synagogue, the man who arranged its services. Paul names Crispus among the few he baptized himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).
The Greek mikron occurs seven times in John 16:16–19. The repetition shows how puzzled the disciples were, and how gently Jesus stays with their question.

Acts 1:3 speaks of forty days of appearances, so the Ascension falls on the fortieth day, a Thursday. Many bishops' conferences, including those of India, transfer it to the following Sunday so that the whole people can celebrate it.
altar: Paul's needle and Christ's altar belong together: at every Mass the priest offers bread, “fruit of the earth and work of human hands.” Our work, our tents and tools and kitchens, is carried to the altar and joined to the sacrifice of Christ.

In the “little while” of the Church we do not see the Lord with our eyes, yet he is not absent. Under the signs of bread and wine he is truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, until he comes again.
outline: Hold up a needle and thread. Ask: can a needle preach the Gospel?
Point 1 · Because he was of the same trade
Paul the worker beside Aquila and Priscilla.
Point 2 · Next door to the synagogue
Rejection, perseverance, and Crispus who believed.
A tent-maker's workshop in Corinth at dusk, the work laid down, and three friends praying together over bread.
live: Do your work today, at home, office, field or school, as carefully as if Christ were your customer. Offer it to him at the start.
Think of someone who rejected your faith or your kindness. Do not cut them off; stay near, pray for them, keep the door open.
Write down one sorrow you are carrying now. Pray over it: Lord, turn this pain into joy, in your time.
fathers: This “little while” is the whole space of the present age. It seems long to us while it lasts; when it is over, we shall see how short it was. Let us wait for the joy that no one can take from us.
Paul was not ashamed to sit in a workshop and stitch skins, and from that workshop he spoke to the world. The needle did not lessen the apostle; it showed his greatness.

Idleness is the enemy of the soul. Let the brothers be busy at fixed times with the work of their hands, and at other times with sacred reading; then they are truly monks, when they live by the labour of their hands, like our fathers and the apostles.
magis: Human work proceeds directly from persons created in the image of God; by work we share in the work of creation, and work united to Christ can be redemptive.
Work is for the human person, not the person for work; Jesus the carpenter shows the dignity of every kind of labour.
Christian hope unfolds from the beginning of Jesus' preaching; it sustains us in the time of trial and opens us to the joy of heaven.
The Church remembers the spiritual bond that ties the people of the New Covenant to Abraham's stock; what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews, then or now.
The Ascension: the risen Christ enters into divine glory and is seated at the right hand of the Father, from where he will come again.
saints: A pupil of St John Bosco in Turin, who died in 1857 aged fourteen and was canonized in 1954. His resolution at his First Communion was “death rather than sin.” The Salesian family keeps his feast on 6 May; he is a patron of choirboys and of expectant mothers.
7 May: First Friday; the novena to the Holy Spirit may begin. 9 May: THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD (in India); World Communications Day. 10 May: St John of Avila (optional). 11 May: Easter weekday.
2027-05-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, you said to your friends: a little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me. We live in that little while. When we weep and mourn, stay near us; when the world laughs at our faith, keep us steady; and turn our pain into joy, as you turned the cross into the tree of life. Bless the work of our hands, as you blessed Paul and Aquila and Priscilla in their workshop. Let our labour be a witness, our homes be open, and our hearts be patient until we see you face to face. You live and reign with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: In Corinth Paul lived and worked as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, and preached in the synagogue every sabbath.
When some opposed him he went next door; Crispus, the synagogue official, believed with all his household.
Jesus: a little while, and you will not see me; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
2027-05-06.action: Offer your day's work to Christ before you begin it, and do one task with special care for his sake.
2027-05-06.question: Which pain in my life am I waiting for the Lord to turn into joy?
catechism: Hope that sustains us in trial.
kidsaint: Dominic was a boy in Italy who went to Don Bosco's school. He was cheerful, loved games, and was a good friend to everyone. Once he stopped two boys who were going to fight with stones by holding up a small cross between them. He died when he was only fourteen. Lesson: you do not have to be grown up to be a saint; you can be holy and happy today.
2027-05-06.special: Easter weekday in India. Where the Ascension is kept today (the Vatican and many countries), it is a solemnity and holy day of obligation; in India it is celebrated on Sunday 9 May. Regina Caeli at noon.
term: A solemnity moved from its own day to another day, by the rules of the liturgical calendar or a decision of the bishops. The Ascension, the Epiphany and Corpus Christi are transferred to a Sunday in India so that all the faithful can take part.

family.explain: Jesus told his friends: soon you will be sad because you will not see me, but your sadness will turn into joy. It is like waiting for a baby to be born: there is pain first, then great happiness. When we are sad, Jesus is still with us, and he can turn our sad days into happy ones.
family.intention: We pray for everyone in our family and our street who is sad today, and for all who work hard with their hands to feed their families.
family.ask: Ask: “What job did each of us do today? Can we offer it to Jesus?” Then say together: Jesus, we give you our work.

illus: In a coastal parish near Alappuzha a retired tailor kept a small shop near the church. He mended school uniforms at half price and never sent anyone away. When a young man who had stopped going to church came to have his trousers altered, the tailor talked with him while he measured and stitched, every week, about cricket, about his mother, and now and then about Jesus. He never preached. After a year the young man asked him to be his sponsor for Confirmation. At the parish feast he said: I did not come back because of a sermon. I came back because of a needle.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, in the little while of our waiting, stay with us and turn our sorrow into joy. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them (Acts 18:3). How can my daily work become a place of witness?
Crispus became a believer in the Lord, together with all his household (Acts 18:8). Whose conversion am I praying for?
Your pain will turn into joy (John 16:20). Where have I seen God turn pain into joy, in my life or in someone else's?
pm.resp: The Lord has revealed to the nations his saving power.
interc: For all workers, especially daily-wage labourers, migrant workers and those without secure work, that their labour may be respected and justly paid.
For Christian couples who serve the Church together, like Aquila and Priscilla.
For good relations between Christians and Jews, and for an end to every form of antisemitism.
For all who are weeping and mourning today, that their pain may be turned into joy.
For our group, that we may wait for the Lord with patience and witness to him in our work.
pm.close: Father, your Son has gone ahead of us, and we wait in hope. Bless the work of our hands and turn our sorrows into the joy of the Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, when we think of St Paul we imagine a great preacher in a crowded city square. Today's reading shows us something else: a man sitting in a workshop in Corinth, stitching leather for tents. Because he was of the same trade, he stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, and they worked together (Acts 18:3).

Paul could have asked the Christians to support him. Often he refused. He wanted no one to think the Gospel was a business. So he worked with his hands by day and preached by night and on the sabbath. His workshop became a chapel, and his customers heard about Jesus while they waited for their tents.

Not everyone listened. Some in the synagogue opposed him. Paul shook out his clothes, a sign that he had done his part. But see where he went: to the house next door. He did not slam the door; he stayed close. And the official of the synagogue himself, Crispus, believed with his whole household (Acts 18:8). Never give up on anyone.

In the Gospel Jesus prepares his friends for a time of sorrow: a little while, and you will no longer see me. You will weep and mourn, but your pain will turn into joy (John 16:20). Not replaced by joy; turned into joy. God does not throw away our tears. He changes them, as he changed Good Friday into Easter.

Today, in many countries, Christians celebrate the Ascension, the day the apostles stopped seeing Jesus with their eyes. In India we will celebrate it on Sunday. But we are all living in that little while now: we do not see him, yet we believe, we work, we wait.

So take your work today, your kitchen, your field, your office, your studies, and offer it to Christ. Take your sorrows and give them to him too. In his time, every pain offered to him will turn into joy, a joy no one can take from you. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, St Paul had a job! He made tents with his friends Aquila and Priscilla. While he worked, he told people about Jesus.
Jesus said: you will be sad for a little while, but then your sadness will turn into joy. When you feel sad, tell Jesus. He can turn your sad face into a smiling face!

intro: Theme: “Your pain will turn into joy.”
Paul the tentmaker, a door kept open next to the synagogue, and the little while in which the Church waits for her Lord.

points.h: Because he was of the same trade
sub: A Jewish couple expelled from Rome.
A workshop that became a chapel.
Work that does not burden others.
q: The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and keep it.
You remember our labor and toil, brothers and sisters; we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
points.apply: Before starting work each day this week, make the sign of the cross and offer the work to Christ by name.

sub: Not walking away, but staying near.
q: I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
Crispus, the official of the synagogue, became a believer in the Lord, together with all his household; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul became believers and were baptized.
points.apply: Pray every day this week for one person who has rejected your faith, and do them one quiet kindness.

sub: Pain that is turned, not thrown away.
q: For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you.
Very truly, I tell you, you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
points.apply: Bring one present sorrow to the Lord in the Blessed Sacrament this week and leave it with him.

concl: Paul preached Christ from a workshop, kept his door open to those who opposed him, and saw a synagogue official come to faith.
We live in the Church's little while between the Ascension and the Lord's return; offered to him, our work becomes witness and our pain becomes joy.
2027-05-06.resolve: Offer your work to Christ each morning this week, and give him one sorrow to turn into joy.
